newsitem.title: USA: Soybean prices lead grains lower, oil markets rise.
newsitem.headline: Soybean prices lead grains lower, oil markets rise.

text.p: Soybean prices fell sharply on Wednesday on concerns that U.S. prices had surged too high for the world market.

In other markets, energy prices rose strongly on forecasts for colder weather while grains and cotton prices fell. The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 commodity futures closed down 2.01 points at 245.13 points.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, May soybeans fell 27 cents a bushel to close at $8.28-1/2, sparked by news that a trading house had sold 45,000 metric tons of soybeans from Brazil -- a main U.S. rival for soybean exports -- for shipment to a customer in the United States who had sought lower prices.

The United States is dominant in soybean production, accounting for half of the annual 137 million ton production. But futures prices this week soared to 8-1/2 year highs on continuing heavy demand for soybeans to produce feed and industrial oils.
"Brazil is on stream now, not just to Europe and the Pacific Rim but to us, too," said grain analyst Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.

The trading house, Glencore Brazil, said it sold the cargo of soybeans to a U.S. firm for April or May shipment. U.S. exporters said the deal made economic sense because Brazilian soybeans were better quality and cheaper than U.S. supplies.
"It's one thing for Brazil to be selling to China or Thailand or Vietnam," another trader said. "It's another when they're coming into U.S. markets."

Some traders said the sale proved U.S. soybeans were no longer competitive and prices would have to move lower. The Philippines rejected a purchase of 15,000 tons of U.S. soybeans on Wednesday due to high prices.
The heavy selling in soybeans by speculators spilled over to other markets, including corn, wheat and cotton.

May corn closed down 11-1/4 cents a bushel at $2.94-1/2, with traders citing reports that Chinese corn exports may double to two million tons this year. That would further erode U.S. corn sales to key buyers like South Korea.

May wheat closed down 3 cents a bushel at $3.79 on the rout in the nearby soybean pit after trading higher most of the day on talk that soft red winter wheat acreage may be lower than expected this year.
Cotton -- a competing oilseed to soybeans -- fell sharply on the New York Cotton Exchange, with May cotton closing down 1.50 cents a pound at 76.15 cents.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed higher as forecasts for colder weather in the northeastern United States overshadowed U.S. oil inventory data which showed higher than expected stocks of crude oil.
April crude oil closed up 51 cents a barrel at $20.62, with April heating oil up 1.25 cents a gallon at 54.08 cents and April gasoline up 0.77 cent a gallon at 64.63 cents.
The National Weather Service 6-to-10 day forecast for March 18 to 22 called for below to much-below normal temperatures in the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world.

That countered a weekly report from the American Petroleum Institute, the oil industry's trade group, that U.S. crude oil stocks grew 6.84 million barrels in the week ended March 7, compared with expectations for a rise of 3.5 million barrels.
"People had been expecting a build in crude," said Al Lindseth, a trader with GSC Energy in Atlanta, adding that the weather forecast had shifted the day's sentiment.
